analysis.one_liner: Lets Americans buy cheaper FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it legal for individuals to import a 90-day personal supply of FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada — and after three years, from other approved countries — instead of paying US pharmacy prices. It would also let licensed US pharmacies, internet pharmacies, and wholesalers import drugs from Canada under labeling, registration, and anti-counterfeiting rules. The same bill creates a licensing system for internet pharmacies and new FDA powers to detain or refuse unsafe drug shipments. It was introduced by a New Hampshire Republican with one cosponsor, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions and pay US prices, which are typically far higher than Canadian prices for the same drugs. People who currently cross the border or order from Canadian pharmacies without clear legal protection would get a legal, defined pathway: a 90-day personal supply carried in person, bought from a licensed Canadian pharmacy, with a valid prescription [S2][S3]. Patients using internet pharmacies would also gain a public list of licensed, inspected sellers, replacing a market full of anonymous websites [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People who fill prescriptions in the US

how_it_helps.text: Allows individuals to legally import up to a 90-day supply of FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada for personal use, purchased from a licensed pharmacy with a valid prescription [S2][S3].

Lets US pharmacies, internet pharmacies, and wholesalers import drugs from Canada starting one year after enactment, with imported drugs clearly labeled as imported and traceable by lot number [S2][S3].

Creates a licensing system for internet pharmacies, with a public list of licensed sellers, so patients can tell legitimate sites from illegal ones; unlicensed pharmacy shipments can be refused and returned at the pharmacy's expense [S3].
Requires credit card networks and banks to build systems that block payments to unlicensed internet pharmacies, cutting off the main way illegal sites get paid [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose sales to cheaper Canadian imports of the same medicines, and importers, who would pay registration and licensing fees to fund FDA oversight. Credit card networks, payment processors, and advertising platforms would bear compliance costs for screening and blocking transactions tied to unlicensed pharmacies [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The safety concern this bill was built to answer is real: imported and internet-sold drugs can be counterfeit or adulterated, which is why the bill adds detention, recall, debarment, and anti-counterfeiting powers for FDA — but those safeguards only work as well as FDA enforcement [S2][S3].
The personal-importation section takes effect immediately upon enactment, before any regulations are written, which leaves less room for regulators to work out the safety details in advance [S3].

The industry's standard objection is that Canadian price controls keep drug prices low there while US sales fund pharmaceutical research, so large-scale importation could pressure drug companies to raise Canadian prices or limit Canadian supply.
The bill layers substantial new regulatory machinery — registration, advance shipment notices, user fees, licensing — whose costs would fall on importers and be passed into drug prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to consumers is straightforward and large: the same FDA-approved pills often cost far less in Canada, and this bill would make buying them legal and traceable. The costs are compliance burdens on industry and an enforcement job for FDA, with a genuine — but regulated — counterfeiting risk. The bill is a pro-importation design with unusually detailed safety provisions, not a loophole; the main honest objection is the immediate effective date for personal importation and the question of whether US demand would strain Canadian supply.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Representative Jeb Bradley of New Hampshire introduced the bill on July 22, 2004, with one Republican cosponsor [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and to its Health Subcommittee, where no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S5].
Congress adjourned on January 3, 2005, and the bill expired with it, never having reached the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who avoided losing sales to cheaper Canadian imports, and American consumers, who kept paying US prices for the same medicines. Canadian pharmacies also lost a chance at a legalized export channel.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor, and it died in a Republican-controlled committee, so there is no roll call showing how the parties would have lined up.

industries.note: Legalized reimportation from Canada means patients could buy the same FDA-approved drugs at Canadian prices, cutting into US sales. The industry fought importation bills of this era on safety grounds.

The bill creates a legal, licensed channel for Canadian and US internet pharmacies to sell to Americans, with a public list of licensees. Licensed sellers gain a market; unlicensed rogue sites can be blocked from payment networks and shut down.

industries.industry: Credit card networks and payment processors
industries.note: They must build systems to identify and block payments to unlicensed internet pharmacies, adding compliance costs. Consumers benefit because rogue pharmacies lose their main way to collect payment.
They become liable for accepting ads from unlicensed internet pharmacies, so they must vet drug ads. This protects consumers from misleading 'no prescription needed' advertising.
